scenario.title: The Second Round - Watergate Part 1

pressureEvents: Wills completes his second round and finds the garage latch taped again — the call to the Second District becomes unavoidable.
McCord's walkie-talkie, volume turned low, fails to carry Baldwin's belated warning before the stairwell door opens.
Officers Shoffler, Barrett, and Leeper reach the sixth-floor landing and begin working the corridor toward Suite 600.

open_threads.historical_record: Wills's contemporaneous Security Officer's Log survives and is public, and it timestamps the rounds: the first discovery at roughly 12:05 to 12:20 AM and the second discovery and police call in a single block reading 1:47 AM to 1:55 AM. What the log does not do is separate the second discovery from the call, so the exact interval between finding the fresh tape and lifting the telephone is not recoverable. Frank Wills never testified before the Senate Select Committee and no committee finding concerning his account exists.

The specific activities the team was conducting inside Suite 600 at the moment the operation was compromised — whether they were replacing a malfunctioning transmitter, photographing documents, or both — was disputed in testimony. McCord testified about the purpose of the second entry, but the precise operational state of the team at the moment of Wills's second discovery was not fully resolved in the public record. The underlying motive for the second entry remains contested among historians; this is a historiographical dispute rather than a documented finding of any congressional committee.

Baldwin's account of his activities in Room 723 during the period immediately before the arrests — specifically how attentively he was monitoring Virginia Avenue and what, if anything, distracted him — rests almost entirely on his own statements to investigators and his October 1972 Los Angeles Times interview. No independent witness corroborated the precise state of his surveillance at the critical interval. The Senate Select Committee did not resolve whether Baldwin's failure to identify the officers in time was the result of inattention, the officers' use of an unmarked vehicle, or the inherent difficulty of the identification task from that distance.

It is established that Wills found tape on the garage-level strike plates a second time after having removed it earlier in the same shift. What has not been definitively established in the public record is whether the tape was replaced by McCord himself — as the most commonly cited account holds — or by another member of the team, and whether it was replaced inadvertently or as a deliberate operational choice. McCord's own explanation, that the tape was replaced to allow the team to exit without being locked in, was accepted by investigators but not independently verified.

Wills's decision to call the Second District rather than simply remove the tape again and continue his rounds has been described in his interviews as straightforward — a second irregularity in the same location in the same night warranted a call. Whether he hesitated, consulted a supervisor, or acted immediately is not established with precision in the documentary record. Wills never testified before the Senate Select Committee, so no congressional examination of this interval exists; his own public accounts have been consistent but were given after the event.

Whether McCord or any member of the team received any warning — from Baldwin, from ambient sound, or from any other source — before the officers reached the sixth floor has never been definitively established. Baldwin testified and told the Los Angeles Times that he did transmit a warning but that it came too late and was not clearly received. McCord's accounts of the moments before the arrests do not describe a clear warning being received and acted upon. The Senate Select Committee noted the communication failure but did not resolve its precise cause.

The log entry itself is public. Wills's Security Officer's Log is held by the National Archives at College Park in the Records of the Watergate Special Prosecution Force, NAID 304970, and the page on which he recorded the break-in has been published in full-resolution page images. The entry reads as a single block, 1:47 AM to 1:55 AM, covering both the discovery and the call. What remains genuinely open is not the existence or content of the entry but its internal order: the log does not say at which minute within that block Wills found the tape or at which minute he telephoned.

The use of an unmarked vehicle without lights or siren by Shoffler, Barrett, and Leeper was consistent with standard plainclothes tactical procedure and was not the result of any specific instruction related to the Watergate call. Their location when dispatched is documented: the car had just passed under the Whitehurst Freeway at approximately 1:52 AM when the dispatcher put out the run, and the officers made a U-turn and reached the Watergate within roughly one to two minutes. What remains open is the interior sequence of the building sweep between arrival and the 2:10 AM arrest.

Baldwin's account of his attempt to identify the three men getting out of the unmarked car on Virginia Avenue is the only account of this moment; no officer involved described being observed from the Howard Johnson. Baldwin told the Los Angeles Times that the men's casual dress initially led him to believe they might not be police. The Senate Select Committee accepted this account but the precise sequence of Baldwin's observations and transmissions in this interval was not reconstructed from any source other than Baldwin himself.

The communication failure between Baldwin and McCord at the critical moment — whether caused by the walkie-talkie's low volume setting, by the lateness of the warning, or by some combination — was acknowledged by both men in their accounts but was never reconstructed with technical precision. McCord testified about the walkie-talkie but did not specify the volume setting at the moment of the warning. The Select Committee's report narrates the breakdown, including Baldwin's radio query about casually dressed men with guns and the reply that "our people are dressed in suits," but it made no formal finding identifying the communication failure as a cause of the arrests.

choice_echoes.historical_record: Wills completed a routine security round in the early hours of June 17, 1972, and discovered tape covering the strike plates on garage-level stairwell doors between roughly 12:05 and 12:20 AM. He removed the tape and continued his round. This first discovery and removal established the baseline that made the second discovery — of fresh tape on the same doors — anomalous enough to prompt a call to police. The sequence is recorded in his own contemporaneous Security Officer's Log, now held by the National Archives.

The team inside the DNC offices was engaged in activities related to the operation's stated purpose of replacing or servicing surveillance equipment and photographing documents. McCord, as the team's security coordinator and the individual responsible for electronic surveillance, was present and working. The walkie-talkie used for communication with Baldwin was kept at low volume to avoid detection. These details are drawn from McCord's testimony and Baldwin's account; the precise activity at the moment of compromise is not established in the record.

Baldwin was stationed in Room 723 of the Howard Johnson Motor Lodge across Virginia Avenue from the Watergate office building. He had binoculars and a walkie-talkie and was responsible for monitoring the street and warning the team of any threat. A television was on in the room; Baldwin's account is that it was on to mask the sound of his radio traffic through the motel wall, and he publicly rejected the claim that he was distracted by a late film as a fabrication. His account is the sole source for the details of his activities and state of alertness during this period.

Wills found tape on the same garage-level strike plates he had cleared earlier in his shift. The tape had been replaced after his first removal. This second discovery, on the same doors, within the same shift, was the direct cause of his decision to call the Metropolitan Police Second District. The replacement of the tape — most commonly attributed to McCord — has been described as the operational error that made the arrests possible.

Wills called the Metropolitan Police Second District. He did not simply remove the tape a second time and continue his round. His decision to treat the second irregularity as a matter for police rather than a routine maintenance issue was the operative choice that set the arrests in motion. The historical record does not document any hesitation or consultation before he made the call.

The historical record does not establish that McCord or any team member received a timely and actionable warning before the officers reached the sixth floor. Baldwin's warning, by his own account, was transmitted but came too late and was not clearly received. The men did attempt to conceal themselves: Officer John Barrett, searching the darkened floor, crouched near a glass-and-wood partition and saw an arm strike the glass inches from his face, drew his weapon and ordered the suspects out, and five men rose from behind a single desk. The number surprised the officers, and Leeper climbed onto a desk to cover the room in case others were hidden. Whether McCord perceived any change in the building's ambient conditions before the officers arrived is not established in testimony.

Wills called the Metropolitan Police Second District between 1:47 and 1:55 AM on June 17, 1972; his Security Officer's Log records the second discovery and the call in a single undivided block and does not separate them. The call initiated the police response that resulted in the arrests at 2:10 AM.

Officers Carl Shoffler, John Barrett, and Paul Leeper responded to the Second District call in an unmarked vehicle, without lights or siren, and in plain clothes, having been roughly a minute away under the Whitehurst Freeway when the run was dispatched at about 1:52 AM. They entered the Watergate building, worked upward through the floors, and arrested the five men inside the DNC offices on the sixth floor at 2:10 AM. The use of an unmarked vehicle in plain clothes was standard procedure for the Second District plainclothes tactical squad.

Baldwin observed three men in casual clothing exit an unremarkable vehicle on Virginia Avenue. By his own account, their dress initially made it difficult to identify them as police officers. He told the Los Angeles Times that he was uncertain whether they were a threat and that this uncertainty delayed his warning transmission. No officer involved described being observed from the Howard Johnson during this approach.

Baldwin transmitted a warning to the team inside the Watergate. By his own account and McCord's, the warning was not received clearly or in time for the team to take any action. McCord's walkie-talkie was set to low volume. The five men were arrested inside the DNC offices. The Select Committee's report narrates this breakdown — Baldwin's radioed description of casually dressed men with guns, and the reply that the team's own people were dressed in suits — but made no formal finding as to its cause.

character_fates.name: Frank Wills

primary_source.citation: Washington Post obituary, September 29, 2000; Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities, Hearings, Book 1 (1973), testimony establishing Wills's role

character_fates.historical_record: Frank Wills continued working as a security guard after the arrests but left the Watergate building; accounts of when vary from July 1972 to sometime in 1973 and no date is firmly established. Accounts of what he received also conflict: one has General Security Services granting him a raise of $2.50 a week, from $80 to $82.50, while another has him quitting because no raise was given. He received no formal recognition. In subsequent years he struggled to find stable employment, in part because of the notoriety attached to his name. He made occasional public appearances related to Watergate anniversaries and gave interviews describing the night of June 17, 1972. He died of a brain tumor on September 27, 2000, at the age of 52; he was living in North Augusta, South Carolina, and sources differ on whether he died there or in Augusta, Georgia.

character_fates.name: James McCord

primary_source.citation: United States v. Liddy et al., D.D.C. (1973); McCord letter to Judge Sirica, March 19, 1973, entered into the public record March 23, 1973; Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities, Hearings, Book 1 (1973)

character_fates.historical_record: James McCord was arrested inside the Watergate complex in the early hours of June 17, 1972, along with the four Miami team members. He was tried before Judge John Sirica and convicted on January 30, 1973, on all eight counts: one count of conspiracy, two counts of burglary, three counts of illegal interception of wire and oral communications, and two counts of possession of intercepting devices. G. Gordon Liddy, tried alongside him, was convicted on six of the eight counts. Facing sentencing, McCord wrote a letter to Judge Sirica on March 19, 1973, alleging that perjury had been committed at trial, that defendants had been pressured to plead guilty and remain silent, and that higher-ups were involved. Sirica read the letter in open court on March 23, 1973. McCord subsequently cooperated with the Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities. Sirica sentenced him to one to five years on November 9, 1973; he entered the federal prison camp at Allenwood, Pennsylvania, in 1975 and served less than four months before release for his cooperation. He published a memoir, 'A Piece of Tape,' in 1974.

character_fates.name: Alfred Baldwin

primary_source.citation: Los Angeles Times, October 5, 1972 (Nelson and Ostrow); Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities, Hearings, Book 1 (1973)

character_fates.historical_record: Alfred Baldwin was not arrested at the Watergate on the night of June 17, 1972. On E. Howard Hunt's instruction he wiped down Room 723 of the Howard Johnson Motor Lodge, loaded the surveillance equipment and the Gemstone file into James McCord's van, and drove the van to McCord's house in Rockville, Maryland. He then left for Connecticut in his own car. The FBI never searched McCord's home and the van's contents were never recovered. He subsequently cooperated with federal investigators and became a government witness. He was not indicted. He gave an extensive account of his role — including his monitoring of telephone conversations from the DNC and his failure to identify the plainclothes officers in time — to the Los Angeles Times, published October 5, 1972, in a piece by Jack Nelson and Ronald Ostrow. He testified before the grand jury and before the Senate Select Committee on May 24, 1973.

character_fates.name: Bernard Barker

primary_source.citation: United States v. Liddy et al., D.D.C. (1973); Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities, Hearings, Book 1 (1973)

character_fates.historical_record: Bernard Barker was arrested inside the Watergate complex on June 17, 1972. He initially pleaded guilty before Judge Sirica on January 15, 1973. After McCord's letter broke the cover story, Barker's cooperation with investigators was limited compared to McCord's. He was sentenced by Sirica and served a period of incarceration. He later returned to Miami, where he remained a figure in the Cuban-American exile community.

character_fates.name: Eugenio Martinez

primary_source.citation: United States v. Liddy et al., D.D.C. (1973); Harper's Magazine, 'Mission Impossible,' Eugenio Martinez, October 1974

character_fates.historical_record: Eugenio Martinez was arrested inside the Watergate complex on June 17, 1972. He pleaded guilty before Judge Sirica on January 15, 1973. He was sentenced and served a period of incarceration. Martinez later wrote about his experience and maintained that he had believed the operation was sanctioned at the highest levels. He was pardoned by President Ronald Reagan on May 13, 1983 — the only one of the five burglars ever pardoned, and the first convicted Watergate figure to receive a presidential pardon. Barker, Sturgis, Gonzalez and McCord were never pardoned.

character_fates.name: Carl Shoffler

primary_source.citation: Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities records; Washington Post reporting on the arrests, June 18, 1972

character_fates.historical_record: Carl Shoffler was one of the three plainclothes officers who responded to the Second District call and made the arrests at the Watergate in the early hours of June 17, 1972 — his twenty-seventh birthday, having been born June 17, 1945. He remained with the Metropolitan Police Department and became a detective. He testified before the Senate Select Committee on May 18, 1973, and gave interviews about the arrests on multiple occasions. He died of pancreatitis on July 13, 1996, at the age of 51.

character_fates.name: Frank Sturgis

primary_source.citation: United States v. Liddy et al., D.D.C. (1973); Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities, Hearings, Book 1 (1973)

character_fates.historical_record: Frank Sturgis was arrested inside the Watergate complex on June 17, 1972. He pleaded guilty before Judge Sirica on January 15, 1973. He was sentenced and served a period of incarceration. Sturgis had a long prior history in anti-Castro paramilitary activities. Whether he ever worked for the CIA is disputed: he claimed such work repeatedly, while the 1975 Rockefeller Commission concluded he "was not an employee or agent of the CIA either in 1963 or at any other time," and the Agency issued a public denial on May 30, 1975. He continued to give interviews about Watergate and related covert operations for the remainder of his life. He died on December 4, 1993, in Miami.

historical_frame.text: The June 17, 1972 break-in was the second entry into the DNC offices at the Watergate; the earlier successful entry took place on May 28, 1972, during which a wiretap was placed on the telephone of DNC executive R. Spencer Oliver, which worked and which Alfred Baldwin then monitored for weeks, and a second device was placed on the telephone of Lawrence O'Brien's secretary, which failed to transmit.
historical_frame.source: Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities, Final Report (1974); Woodward and Bernstein, 'All the President's Men' (1974), citing grand jury and committee records

historical_frame.text: James McCord's letter to Judge John Sirica, read in open court on March 23, 1973, was the first public break in the cover story constructed after the arrests and precipitated the collapse of the White House containment strategy. The Senate had already established the Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities by S. Res. 60 on February 7, 1973, six weeks before the letter; its public hearings opened on May 17, 1973. The letter did not cause the hearings to be held, but it transformed what they would find.
historical_frame.source: McCord letter to Judge Sirica, March 19, 1973, Congressional Record; Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities, Hearings, Book 1 (1973)

historical_frame.text: President Richard Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974, the only U.S. president to have done so; the House Judiciary Committee had approved three articles of impeachment — obstruction of justice, abuse of power, and contempt of Congress — between July 27 and July 30, 1974.
historical_frame.source: House Judiciary Committee, Articles of Impeachment, July 27–30, 1974; Presidential resignation address, August 8, 1974, Public Papers of the Presidents

immediate_outcome.summary: At approximately 2:10 AM on June 17, 1972, Officers Carl Shoffler, John Barrett, and Paul Leeper arrested five men — James McCord, Bernard Barker, Eugenio Martinez, Frank Sturgis, and Virgilio Gonzalez — inside the sixth-floor offices of the Democratic National Committee at the Watergate office building, where the men were found hiding. All five wore surgical gloves; the officers recovered photographic equipment, electronic surveillance devices, and roughly $2,300 in cash, most of it in hundred-dollar bills with serial numbers in sequence. The arrests initiated a chain of events that culminated in the resignation of President Richard Nixon on August 9, 1974.

key_facts.text: Frank Wills found tape on the garage-level stairwell door strike plates for the second time that night and called the Metropolitan Police Second District between 1:47 and 1:55 AM on June 17, 1972; his Security Officer's Log records both events in a single undivided time block and does not separate them.
key_facts.source: Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities, Hearings, Book 1 (1973), testimony of Frank Wills; Washington Post, June 18, 1972

key_facts.text: The three plainclothes officers who responded — Shoffler, Barrett, and Leeper — arrived in an unmarked vehicle and entered the building without lights or siren, which delayed Alfred Baldwin's identification of them as police from his observation post at the Howard Johnson Motor Lodge across Virginia Avenue.
key_facts.source: Los Angeles Times, October 5, 1972 (Nelson and Ostrow); Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities, Hearings, Book 1 (1973)

key_facts.text: Five men were arrested inside the DNC offices: James McCord, Bernard Barker, Eugenio Martinez, Frank Sturgis, and Virgilio Gonzalez. All five were charged with second-degree burglary and possession of implements of crime.
key_facts.source: Washington Post, June 18, 1972; United States v. Liddy et al., D.D.C. (1973)

key_facts.text: Among the items recovered from the arrested men were two sophisticated eavesdropping devices and roughly $2,300 in cash, most of it in hundred-dollar bills with serial numbers in sequence. The bills were traced through the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta to the Republic National Bank of Miami, where Bernard Barker held an account, and through the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia to Girard Bank and Trust; the account itself was subsequently connected to funds of the Committee for the Re-election of the President.
key_facts.source: Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities, Final Report (1974); Washington Post, June 18, 1972

glossary.definition: 1972, when Richard Nixon was seeking re-election against Democrat George McGovern and held a commanding polling lead that made his victory appear certain.
The Watergate building's security guard working the night shift, whose eighty-dollar-a-week salary and job security hinge on his discretion in handling what might be a routine custodian's mistake.
A fixed light fixture mounted above the lobby reception desk that provides the only interior illumination of the Watergate office building's ground floor after hours.
The spring-loaded bolt that extends from a door lock into the strike plate—without it engaging, a door can be opened from the inside at any time.
The metal plate on a doorframe that the latch bolt slides into when a door closes—taping over it prevents the bolt from catching and locking the door.
Adhesive tape used to keep stairwell door latches open so the team can move freely through the building without triggering alarms—discovered by the security guard on multiple rounds.
The specific Howard Johnson hotel room where a lookout has spent eight or nine consecutive nights monitoring audio feeds and watching for security problems across the street.
The hotel across Virginia Avenue from the Watergate office building, where operatives monitored the listening device from an upper-floor room and coordinated the break-in.
A listening device planted in the DNC office in May that had been broadcasting audio to monitors across the street—the 'technical correction' that brings the team back inside on this night.
The administrative headquarters and nerve center of the Democratic Party, occupying the sixth floor of the Watergate complex where campaign strategy, voter files, and internal documents were stored.
New legislation effective April 7, 1972, that required campaigns to report donations publicly—which is why the Committee moved money through intermediary accounts before the deadline.

glossary.term: Committee for the Re-election of the President
glossary.definition: Nixon's official campaign organization in 1972, which raised unprecedented amounts of cash and coordinated financial transfers through Mexico and Miami to avoid the new campaign finance disclosure requirements.

A mixed-use development of office and residential buildings on Virginia Avenue near the Kennedy Center, opened in 1965 on the Potomac's east bank—known simply by its address rather than a proper name.

scenario.description: Washington, D.C., June 17, 1972, twelve minutes before two in the morning. A night guard has found the same tape twice. Five men are working on the sixth floor of the Watergate office building, and the lookout across Virginia Avenue is watching a street that tells him nothing. The macro-outcome is fixed. The ninety minutes before it are yours.

sections.text: It is the summer of a presidential election year, and Richard Nixon leads George McGovern by margins that make the outcome look settled. The Committee for the Re-election of the President has raised more money than any campaign in American history, some of it in cash, some of it moved through accounts in Mexico and Miami before the new campaign finance disclosure law takes effect on April 7. The Democratic National Committee occupies the sixth floor of a glass-and-concrete complex on Virginia Avenue, a building whose name is simply its address — the Watergate — a residential and office development opened in 1965 on the Potomac's east bank, a short walk from the Kennedy Center. Washington in June 1972 is a city that believes it has seen everything, and it has not.

For the five men on the sixth floor, tonight is a technical correction — a transmitter that has been feeding poor audio since May needs to be replaced, and internal campaign documents need to be photographed before the building opens Monday morning. For the man across the street in Room 723, it is the eighth or ninth consecutive night of nothing, and nothing is what he expects. For Frank Wills, what is at stake is narrower and more immediate: eighty dollars a week, a job he cannot afford to lose, and the specific social cost of calling the police over what is probably a custodian's oversight. Nobody in this building, and nobody across the street, understands that the night's outcome will be read in every subsequent decade of American political life.

Virginia Avenue is empty at this hour, the pavement holding the day's heat in a way that makes the air feel used. The Watergate office building's lobby is dark behind its glass facade, the only interior light a security lamp above the reception desk. Across six lanes of asphalt, the Howard Johnson Motor Lodge shows a few lit windows on the upper floors, the television glow of insomnia or a late shift. The Potomac is two blocks west and the night smells of river mud and car exhaust and the particular staleness of a city that has been awake too long. Inside the building, the air conditioning runs at a level calibrated for a full office day, which means it is too cold for one man walking a circuit with a flashlight.

You are at the threshold of ninety minutes that will not feel like history because they do not feel like anything yet — they feel like a shift, a round, a job, a decision about whether to pick up a phone. The tape is there again. The stairwell smells of concrete and motor oil. The flashlight beam catches the adhesive edge, and you are the only person in the building who knows it.

winConditions: As Wills: log the second tape discovery, reach the security phone, and complete the call to the Second District before the round expires.

As McCord: finish replacing the transmitter and clear the team's most compromising pocket litter before the stairwell door opens — the hard floor items cannot be removed, but exposure above the floor can be minimized.
As Baldwin: transmit a warning early enough that McCord receives it on the walkie-talkie before the officers reach the sixth floor.
failConditions: As Wills: second tape is not reported before 2:00 AM, allowing the team additional time to sanitize the suite.
As McCord: transmitter housing is left open and the Miami crew's documents are still spread on the desk when the door opens.
As Baldwin: warning goes out after officers are already on the sixth floor, giving McCord no actionable lead time.
